fact: The square-root function on ℝ is monotone. Applied to a²≤a²+b² and b²≤a²+b², it bounds the two coordinates of the Euclidean product distance.

grounds.reason: The product distance is sqrt(dist(x,y)^2+|t-u|^2). Both squared terms are nonnegative.

justification: Real.sqrt_le_sqrt has only the real inequality premise. Each premise follows by adding a nonnegative square. This is the routine scalar comparison used in the displayed projection argument.

fact: For real a, sqrt(a²)=|a|; for a≥0 this equals a. Thus the square-root comparisons in S001 give dist(x,y) and |t-u| on their left sides.

grounds.reason: dist(x,y) is a nonnegative metric distance; |t-u| is nonnegative. The product distance is the displayed square root.
The comparison is made for arbitrary coordinate pairs, then for points of V_i.

justification: The probed identity is unconditional on a∈ℝ. Substitute a=dist(x,y) and a=|t-u| and simplify absolute values using nonnegativity. Supremum bounds for projected diameters then follow directly from D002. No projection regularity is assumed.

fact: If 0≤a≤b and s≥0, then a^s≤b^s. Here (diam A_i)^s≤ρ_i^s, including at diameter zero.

fact: The nonnegative sum ∑_{i≥0}2^(−i−1) equals 1, and its subseries over K⊆ℕ is at most 1.

grounds.reason: K⊆ℕ and η_i uses the weights 2^(−i−1), with the original natural index i.
Nonnegative sums are suprema of finite partial sums.

justification: Apply ENNReal.tsum_geometric at r=1/2 to obtain sum (1/2)^i=2. Each weight is (1/2)(1/2)^i. Scaling the finite partial sums by the finite positive factor 1/2 scales their supremum, giving 1. Every finite subseries over K is bounded by a full partial sum (take a larger terminal natural index), hence the subseries is at most 1. This verifies the routine numerical series estimate already used in S003.

fact: The splitting, comparison and finite-scalar multiplication of nonnegative series used in S003 follow from their finite-partial-sum definition; all inequalities remain valid when the main (s+1)-cost is infinite.

grounds.reason: A nonnegative series is the supremum of finite partial sums.
ρ_i, η_i and ε are finite and nonnegative, with ε>0.
The pointwise term bounds and nonnegative splitting are explicitly displayed; BG011–BG013 verify the only power/series identities.

justification: Termwise inequalities give inequalities for every finite partial sum and hence their suprema. For sequences a_i,b_i≥0, a common finite index set containing any two finite sets shows sup_F sum_F(a_i+b_i)=sup_F sum_F a_i+sup_F sum_F b_i. In the finite case this follows by approximating each supremum from below and taking the union; in an infinite case arbitrarily large finite sums give the same conclusion. For a finite scalar q≥0, q=0 is immediate and q>0 carries upper bounds and lower approximants between sup_F q sum_F a_i and q sup_F sum_F a_i. Apply this with a_i=ρ_i^(s+1), b_i=η_iρ_i^s and q=ε or 1/2. No exchange of an analytic limit with an integral is added; that exchange is already the direct input M006.

fact: The ε-removal and final infimum give the full exported inequality, with empty and infinite costs handled.

grounds.reason: F001 supplies c<∞.
F003 gives c≤T+ε for all ε>0, with T the original cover's nonnegative (s+1)-cost.
H^(s+1)_δ(F) is the infimum over exactly all countable δ-covers, with infimum of an empty family equal to ∞.

justification: If T=∞, c≤T. If T<∞ and c>T, choose ε=(c−T)/2>0 in F003 to contradict c≤T+ε. Dropping empty cover members preserves cost because s+1>0. Consequently c is a lower bound for every admissible cover cost. By the defining greatest-lower-bound property c≤their infimum; if there are no covers it is c≤∞. The proof never needs a minimizing cover or an interchange of infimum and integral.
